accepted.reason: Good observation-target alignment: hospitalization rate plausibly lags an infectious proxy, and delayed_I is explicitly recommended. Parsimonious for n_train=31 and single-season dynamics; avoids adding an H compartment that is noted as weakly identifiable in short series. Delay=2 also matches one of the current discovery patterns.

Observation map I+H is among recommended maps and can hedge against mis-specifying whether the reported rate behaves more like admissions vs burden/occupancy. However, with a hospitalization-rate target, mixing I risks shape/level mismatch and persistence inflation; still acceptable as a robustness check without fractional memory.

SEIR with delayed_I remains parsimonious and can be a useful sensitivity check on whether waning immunity is actually needed over this single season. But delay=3 may be less plausible for weekly admissions and can over-shift peaks; also risks underfitting if there is noticeable late-season persistence that SEIRS would capture.

rejected.reason: Although H aligns semantically with hospitalization rate, adding an explicit H compartment in SEIHR increases complexity and identifiability risk for a short single-season series (n_train=31), consistent with the stated risk note. Likely to create unstable separation between I and H timing/scale without strong information in the data.

Fractional memory adds flexibility that is hard to justify with 31 training points and moderate peakiness; high risk of overfitting and weak identifiability of the fractional parameter. Also, delayed_I with delay=1 conflicts with the stronger plausibility of ~2-week lag already supported by current discovery patterns.

suggested_edits.edit: Clarify whether the observation is intended to approximate admissions vs occupancy/burden; if it is admissions, consider down-weighting I in the I+H map (conceptually) or explicitly stating that I+H is a robustness proxy rather than a mechanistic admission model.

Consider narrowing the delay to 2 weeks (or explicitly justify 3 weeks with surveillance/reporting rationale) to reduce peak-timing misalignment risk; keep SEIR as a simplicity sensitivity check rather than a primary mechanistic choice.
